disposition_reason: Both ancient accounts describe the decisive defeat of the revolt but neither names the place, so it is drawn as a halo over the Watling Street corridor in the Midlands, not a pin.
title: The final defeat of Boudica's revolt
candidate_description: Suetonius Paulinus, with a much smaller force, chose a defile backed by woodland and defeated the rebel army; Boudica died soon after (by poison in Tacitus, by illness in Dio).
place: Probably along Watling Street, English Midlands (site unknown)
uncertainty_note: Neither Tacitus nor Dio names the site. It is usually placed on or near Watling Street between London and Wroxeter; candidates include Mancetter (Manduessedum) and High Cross on the Warwickshire/Leicestershire border and Church Stowe in Northamptonshire, and some writers argue for sites well outside this halo. No battlefield archaeology has been confirmed. Tacitus's figures (80,000 Britons, 400 Romans killed) are not taken as reliable. The revolt is dated AD 60 or 61: Tacitus places it (with the attack on Mona) under the consuls of 61, but many scholars read his annalistic grouping as covering 60–61 and put the outbreak in 60; the atlas uses 60 (circa) for every revolt row.
facets: Evidence type=ancient narratives|Dating basis=historical narrative|Interpretation=on or near Watling Street; Mancetter often proposed

disposition_reason: A winter camp named in the Chronicle and identified on the ground by excavation beside St Wystan's church; drawn as a pin.
title: The 'great army' winters at Repton
candidate_description: The Viking army moved from Lindsey to Repton, took winter quarters there in 873–4 and drove King Burgred of Mercia from his kingdom. Excavation found a ditched enclosure using the church as part of its circuit, Scandinavian-style burials and a large charnel deposit.
uncertainty_note: The Chronicle enters the wintering under 874 (its year began in autumn in this section), so the stay is given as the winter of 873–4. That the charnel deposit and the D-shaped enclosure belong to the army is an interpretation; radiocarbon redating (Jarman et al. 2018) supports it for the charnel.

uncertainty_note: The account comes from sources written at Chester-le-Street and Durham between the 10th and 12th centuries. disposition_reason: A battle recorded by the Chronicle and Asser; the site 'Ethandun' is usually identified with Edington in Wiltshire but not proved, so it is drawn as a halo.
title: Battle of Edington (Ethandun)
candidate_description: Alfred of Wessex gathered the men of Somerset, Wiltshire and part of Hampshire at Egbert's Stone, advanced to Ethandun and defeated Guthrum's army, which then gave hostages; Guthrum was baptised soon afterwards.
uncertainty_note: The battle is secure. Ethandun is usually identified with Edington below the northern scarp of Salisbury Plain (Wiltshire), which fits the route via Egbert's Stone and Iley Oak, but no battlefield archaeology confirms it; Edington on the Polden Hills in Somerset has also been proposed. The month is inferred from the Chronicle's 'seventh week after Easter' (Easter fell on 23 March in 878), so early to mid May.
facets: Evidence type=annal and biography|Dating basis=annal; liturgical reckoning|Interpretation=Ethandun identified with Edington, Wiltshire

disposition_reason: The battle is certain but its site is disputed; drawn as a halo on the Wirral, the leading candidate, with other proposals named in the note.
title: Battle of Brunanburh
candidate_description: Æthelstan and his brother Edmund defeated a combined army of Olaf Guthfrithson of Dublin, Constantine II of Alba and the Strathclyde Britons.
uncertainty_note: The battle is well attested but no source locates Brunanburh securely. Bromborough on the Wirral, whose name derives from Brunanburh, is the leading candidate, and metal-detected 10th-century finds around Brimstage, Clatterbridge and Storeton have been offered in support but are not yet fully published. Other proposals include Burnswark (Dumfriesshire), Lanchester (Co. Durham) and sites in Yorkshire and Lancashire. The halo covers the Wirral proposal only.
